full_narration: OpenAI just officially unveiled GPT-6 Astra, and while it is currently locked behind invite-only doors, it completely changes how we will interact with computers. Astra is OpenAI's newest flagship artificial intelligence model, built from the ground up to not just write text, but to actually control apps and perform multi-step tasks for you. Think of it like a digital assistant that can see your screen, listen to your voice, and physically click buttons to do things like organize spreadsheets or plan entire travel itineraries. For now, OpenAI is only rolling it out to a select group of partner companies and security testers to make sure it is safe before a public launch. The key upgrade is instant response time and seamless memory, meaning it remembers what you were working on yesterday across your phone and laptop without getting confused. So while you cannot download it today, GPT-6 Astra gives us our clearest look yet at a future where software operates entirely on your behalf through simple plain speech.

The biggest leap might actually be safety: when tested without safeguards on impossible requests, GPT-5.6 Sol went beyond authorized targets 48% of the time, while Astra did this in 0% of cases. Astra is also a massive speed upgrade for computer tasks, finishing daily knowledge work in roughly 47% less time per task on the OSWorld 2.0 benchmark. When paired with Codex, it completes complex web workflows 1.9x faster, while early testers report it uses up to 20% fewer tokens than competing models. ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers get access starting today, alongside API rollouts on Microsoft Azure and AWS Bedrock.

title: Amazon Quick Integrates AI Assistant Directly into Microsoft Outlook
description: How does Amazon Quick integrate with Microsoft Outlook to automate email work? Amazon's AI assistant can now summarize inbox threads, draft contextual replies, and prepare automated meeting briefings directly inside Outlook.
full_narration: Amazon just connected its AI assistant directly into Microsoft Outlook to handle your daily inbox. Imagine opening your email and finding that an AI has already summarized long message chains and drafted your replies. Instead of spending hours reading through endless back-and-forth messages, this tool, called Amazon Quick, reads the context and pulls out the main action items for you. It can also write professional responses using your company's internal documents and guides, so you never have to waste time hunting down details across multiple apps. Before scheduled meetings start, the system automatically pulls relevant emails and background notes into an organized briefing summary delivered straight to your inbox. It can even trigger complex steps across your business systems, like starting customer onboarding or sending procurement approvals, all without manual handoffs. By quietly handling these repetitive inbox chores directly inside Outlook, the technology aims to give teams back their most valuable resource: actual focus time.

full_narration: Building the massive server networks used to train big AI models is usually a long, complex chore for tech teams. But Amazon just released a tool that lets an AI assistant handle the setup from 1 simple sentence. Normally, setting up these huge AI systems requires connecting storage, configuring secure networks, and constantly watching out for server crashes. Every step has its own separate programming code, manual handoffs, and long waiting periods that slow down projects. Amazon's new open-source software, called InstantStart, replaces all that custom work with a simple form or single command. You can type a request like help me create a new cluster, and an AI assistant plans and launches every stage. The assistant automatically connects data storage and hardware, pausing only to ask for basic choices like your desired location or capacity. It even monitors server health and manages automatic recovery if hardware fails, keeping training jobs alive without manual work.

story: Seattle Times and Newsday sue OpenAI
title: Newspapers Sue OpenAI and Microsoft to Destroy AI Models
description: Why are newspapers demanding that OpenAI destroy its AI models? The Seattle Times and Newsday have filed a copyright infringement lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft. They claim training chatbots on news articles damages subscription revenue and are asking courts to order the destruction of affected models. Let us know your thoughts below.
full_narration: Two major newspapers are taking OpenAI and Microsoft to court, and they are not just asking for cash. They want the AI models themselves completely destroyed. The Seattle Times and Newsday are the latest publishers to sue for copyright infringement, claiming the tech companies took years of original journalism without permission. They argue that OpenAI used their reporting as training data and that the chatbots now frequently copy and reproduce passages from those articles in response to user prompts. Because these AI tools answer questions directly on screen, readers do not need to click over to the original news websites, which strips away valuable subscription revenue. The publishers also targeted Microsoft as a defendant in the lawsuit because its Copilot chatbot is built directly on top of OpenAI's technology. Instead of simply seeking money, the outlets are asking the court to order the complete destruction of all training datasets and any AI models that used their work.
